blocks.main: **The air in the vocal tract is a fixed-free system that vibrates longitudinally, back and forth along the tube.** The tube runs from the vocal folds to the lips. The vocal folds are closed, so the air there cannot move, and that end is **fixed**. The lips are open, so the air there moves freely, and that end is **free**.
sub: The air moves along the tube, not up and down inside the mouth.
This air moves the same way a **building** sways, and the math for both is almost exactly the same.
So the frequencies of the air are **formants**, which are odd multiples of the lowest one. **F1** is the lowest mode, and **F2** is the next mode.
The modes look like a building's modes turned on their side. The fixed glottis end is on the left, and the free lip end is on the right.
blocks.end: That is why changing the mass and stiffness of the air moves the formants and makes different vowels and consonants.

blocks.main: **The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a chain of masses and springs.** The chain is fixed at the glottis and free at the lips. The masses stand for the air's **inertia**, which is its resistance to being moved. The springs stand for the air's **springiness**.
sub: The lowest mode of the chain matches **F1**, and the next mode matches **F2**.
The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**, and the frequencies of a fixed-fixed system are called **harmonics**.
The second mode holds three quarter-wave pieces, so it vibrates **three times faster** than the first.
The masses near the free end move very freely in both modes, because nothing holds them in place.
blocks.end: So the chain shows where the air acts as a mass and where it acts as a spring.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p23 · Lecture 13 · p11 · Lecture 14 · p6
blocks.main: **The air in the tube can also be modeled as lines of air particles, whose spacing shows what the air does.** Each particle stands for billions of real air molecules. The closed vocal folds sit at the fixed end, and the open lips sit at the free end.
sub: Where the lines come very close together and then spread far apart, the air is **compressing and expanding**, so it acts like a **spring**.
Where the lines move back and forth without changing their spacing, the air acts like a **mass**. This is easiest to see at the lips, where the air simply moves in and out.
At the fixed end, the air cannot move, but it compresses and expands a lot.
blocks.end: So bunching and spreading means springiness, and sliding without bunching means mass.

blocks.main: **In every mode, the air at the closed end is always springy, and the air at the open end is always moving.** Air can be compressed against a closed end. At an open end there is nothing to compress it against, so the air just moves back and forth.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air near the closed glottis end compresses and expands a lot. The air near the open lip end moves back and forth.
In **Mode 2**, the air compresses a lot at the closed end and again about two-thirds of the way along. About one-third of the way along, the air mostly moves.
In higher modes, springy places and moving places **take turns** more and more times along the tube.
blocks.end: So the first step for any vowel is knowing where the air moves and where it compresses in each mode.

blocks.main: **The modes of the air match the modes of a building, and each higher mode adds one more point of no motion.** **F1** has one point of no motion, at the fixed end. **F2** has two, one at the fixed end and one inside the tube. **F3** has three.
sub: Between the points of no motion, places of most motion and places of most compression take turns, just as on a vibrating string.
A building in **Mode 1** matches the air, with lots of compression near the ground and lots of motion near the top.
In **Mode 4** of a building, the springiest places are the four places that do not move. These are the fixed bottom and the three points where the building crosses its resting position.
Raising stiffness where the building moves the most changes **nothing**, because it is not acting like a spring there. Raising stiffness where it does not move makes the frequency **go up a lot**.
blocks.end: So the points of no motion are the springiest places, because the air there compresses and expands the most.

blocks.main: **The schwa, the central vowel with no constriction, matches the prediction for a uniform fixed-free tube.** A uniform tube predicts that F2 is three times F1 and F3 is five times F1. A measured schwa had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 Hz**, which are those odd multiples.
sub: Every other vowel moves the formants away from these schwa values, because it changes where the air moves and where it compresses.
blocks.end: So the schwa values are the starting point for describing every other vowel.

blocks.main: **A constriction raises both the stiffness and the mass of the air, and the two effects do not cancel out.** Compressed air becomes **stiffer**, the same way pressing on a tire makes it stiffer. A constriction also packs the air into a smaller space, which raises its **density**, so the air is more massive and harder to move.
sub: Canceling out only happens for a single mass on a single spring. In a system with many masses and springs, each spot in a mode is either mostly **moving** or mostly **stretching**.

At a spot with no motion and lots of stretching, only the extra stiffness counts, so the frequency **goes up**. At a spot with lots of motion and no stretching, only the extra mass counts, so the frequency **goes down**.
Speech proves the effects do not cancel, because constrictions in different places clearly change the frequencies of the voice.

Adding mass and stiffness at the very top of a building **lowers every mode**, including Mode 4. The top is the free end, so in every mode it moves the most and is almost never stretched. So only the extra mass counts there.
blocks.end: That is why rounding the lips lowers every formant, because the lip end of the vocal tract matches the top of the building.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p15 · Lecture 13 · p15 · Lecture 14 · p7, 10, 14
blocks.main: **Any constriction question is answered by finding what the air at that spot does in each mode.** A constriction always adds both mass and stiffness. Where the air mostly moves, the extra mass counts and the formant goes down. Where the air mostly compresses, the extra stiffness counts and the formant goes up.
sub: At a spot where the air in **Mode 3** bunches and spreads but hardly moves, the air acts like a **pure spring**. The extra mass does not matter there, so only the extra stiffness counts, and **F3 goes up**. The answer is built one step at a time, with each step resting on the one before.
The same spot can be moving in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2. Then one constriction lowers F1 and raises F2 at the same time, so each mode must be checked separately.
Three spots along the tube matter for vowels. **/a/** is one-third of the way from the glottis, **/i/** is two-thirds of the way, and **/u/** is at the lips.

At the lips, the air moves in both modes, so **/u/ lowers both formants**. Two-thirds along, the air moves in Mode 1 and is springy in Mode 2, so **/i/ lowers F1 and raises F2**. One-third along, the air is springy in Mode 1 and moving in Mode 2, so **/a/ raises F1 and lowers F2**.
blocks.end: So a vowel is identified by its pair of formants, not by one formant alone.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p16 · Lecture 13 · p12 · Lecture 14 · p8
blocks.main: **Vowels differ in the shape of the vocal tract, which depends on where the tongue or lips make a constriction.** A **constriction** is a narrowing of the tract. Images taken while people speak show where it occurs between the closed glottis and the open lips. Distances are measured from the **glottis**, the space between the vocal folds at the fixed end.
sub: In **done**, there is no significant constriction, so the tract is fairly uniform along its whole length.
In **dean**, the vowel is **high front**, because the constriction is under the roof of the mouth. That spot is about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Don**, the vowel is **low back**, because the constriction is far back in the throat. That spot is about **one-third of the way from the glottis**.
In **dune**, **lip rounding** makes the constriction **at the lips**, so the vowel is **high back**. In **Dan**, the tongue is low and toward the front, so the vowel is **low front**.
blocks.end: So the same voice from the vocal folds can become different vowels, because each constriction changes the formants.

blocks.main: **A constriction always raises both the inertia and the stiffness of the air at that spot.** **Inertia** is the air's resistance to being moved, which is its mass. **Stiffness** is how hard the air pushes back when it is compressed. In the mass-spring model, a constriction is drawn as **heavier masses and stiffer springs** at that spot.
sub: Compressing air raises its stiffness, the same way compressing the air in a tire makes it stiffer. So a constriction where the air compresses a lot **raises the frequency**.
A constriction packs the air into a smaller space, which raises its **density** and so its mass. So a constriction where the air moves a lot **lowers the frequency**.
The two effects do not cancel, because moving places and compressing places take turns. At one spot in one mode, only the extra mass or only the extra stiffness counts.
blocks.end: So the effect of a constriction depends on what the air is doing at that spot in each mode.

blocks.main: **Two questions, asked in order, answer any constriction question.** The first asks whether the air at the spot is mostly moving or mostly compressing in that mode. The second asks which change counts there, the extra mass or the extra stiffness.
sub: On a string fixed at both ends, mass and stiffness are added at one small spot. At that spot, **Mode 3** crosses its middle line and **Mode 4** is at the top of a bump.
In **Mode 3**, the string does not move there but is stretched the most. So only the extra stiffness counts, and **the frequency goes up**.
In **Mode 4**, the string moves the most there and hardly stretches. So only the extra mass counts, and **the frequency goes down**.

A formant change also tells what the air was doing. If a constriction raises a formant a lot, the air there must be **very springy and hardly moving** in that mode. If it lowers a formant a lot, the air there must be **moving a lot**.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p16, 19 · Lecture 13 · p12 · Lecture 14 · p8, 11
blocks.main: **In done, the vowel is schwa, and its formants are the starting point for every other vowel.** The tract has no significant constriction, so no extra mass or stiffness is added at any spot.
sub: In **Mode 1** and **Mode 2**, nothing is added anywhere, so neither extra counts and **F1 and F2 stay at the uniform-tube values**.
Schwa's formants are about **500, 1500 and 2500 Hz**, and the other vowels move the formants away from these values.
blocks.end: So each other vowel is described by how its constriction moves F1 and F2 away from schwa.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p19 · Lecture 13 · p16 · Lecture 14 · p11
blocks.main: **For /u/, as in dune, F1 and F2 both go down.** **Lip rounding** makes the constriction at the lips, which is the **free end** of the tube. At the open end, the air moves back and forth with almost no compression in every mode, so it acts as a pure mass.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at the lips is moving, so the extra mass counts and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at the lips is also moving, so the extra mass counts and **F2 goes down**.
The extra stiffness does not matter in either mode, because the air at the lips is moving, not stretching.
A speaker went from the central vowel, near 500, 1500 and 2500 Hz, into /u/, and **both formants dropped**. A measured /u/ had an F1 in the low two hundreds, well below 500.
blocks.end: So at the lips only the extra mass matters, because the air there moves the most in every mode.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p20 · Lecture 13 · p17 · Lecture 14 · p12
blocks.main: **For /i/, as in dean, F1 goes down and F2 goes up.** The constriction is about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**, near the front of the tract. That one spot acts differently in the two modes.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot moves back and forth with hardly any compression, so it acts like a mass. The extra mass counts, so **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot compresses and expands a lot, so it acts like a spring. The extra stiffness counts, so **F2 goes up**.
A speaker went from schwa into /i/, and the **first formant dropped a lot** while the **second formant went up**.
blocks.end: So the formants of /i/ **move apart**, because one constriction sits on a moving spot for F1 and a springy spot for F2.

blocks.ref: Lecture 12 · p21 · Lecture 13 · p18 · Lecture 14 · p13
blocks.main: **For /a/, as in Don, F1 goes up and F2 goes down, which is the reverse of /i/.** The constriction is about **one-third of the way from the glottis**, toward the back of the throat.
sub: In **Mode 1**, that spot is close enough to the closed end that the air is mostly compressed and springy. The extra stiffness counts, so **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, that spot sits between two springy regions, so the air there mostly moves. The extra mass counts, so **F2 goes down**.
A speaker producing /a/ showed **F1 going up and F2 going down**.
blocks.end: So the formants of /a/ **move toward each other**, and in a typical /a/ F1 and F2 are fairly close together.

blocks.main: **The spectra of /i/ and /a/ show the same harmonics shaped by two different filters.** The harmonics from the vocal folds are the same under both vowels. Moving the constriction moves the formants, so it changes which harmonics are loud.
sub: In the /i/ spectrum, the tall harmonics are bunched at the very bottom. A long stretch of short harmonics follows, and the next tall group is much higher up. So **F1 is low and F2 is high**, and the two are far apart.
In the /a/ spectrum, the first two groups of tall harmonics sit **close together** in the lower part. That is because F1 is raised and F2 is lowered.
blocks.end: So only the filter differs between /i/ and /a/, and the filter is set by where the constriction is.

blocks.main: **Speech uses two vibrating systems at the same time, a source and a filter.** The **vocal folds** are a fixed-fixed system and act as the **source**, so they produce **harmonics**. The **air in the vocal tract** is a fixed-free system and acts as the **filter**, so its frequencies are the **formants**.
sub: The lowest harmonic is the **base frequency**, or **F0**, and the other harmonics fall at whole-number multiples of it. In one example the harmonics are **100 Hz apart**.
For the schwa, the formants are near **500, 1500, 2500 and 3500 Hz**.
The vocal folds decide which frequencies are present, and the shape of the mouth decides which of those frequencies are loud.

blocks.main: **The mass and stiffness of the vocal folds set F0, and F0 sets the spacing of the harmonics.** More mass lowers F0, and more stiffness raises it. With an F0 of 150 Hz, the first five harmonics are 150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz.
sub: **Big, heavy, loose vocal folds** have a large mass and a small stiffness, so their **F0 is low**. It is around 100 Hz, with harmonics at 200, 300 and so on.
**Tighter, lighter vocal folds** have a higher F0, such as 250 Hz, with harmonics at 500 and 750 Hz.
**Very tight, light vocal folds** have an even higher F0, such as 350 Hz, with harmonics at 700 and 1050 Hz.

F0 can be measured in **Praat** by viewing a spectral slice of a short piece of speech and picking the lowest harmonic. One measured voice had an F0 around 170 Hz, and the next harmonic was at about twice that value.
blocks.end: So a higher F0 spaces the harmonics farther apart.

blocks.main: **F0 keeps changing while people talk, and listeners use the changes to understand meaning.** Only a robot keeps F0 constant. Speakers change F0 by tightening and loosening the vocal folds with the muscles of the larynx.
sub: When "The dog slept here" is a statement, F0 **falls** at the very end. When the same words are a question, F0 **rises** at the end.
The way F0 moves also tells listeners whether a person is being sarcastic, pretending or even lying.

blocks.main: **The filter decides how loud each harmonic is, and a formant makes the harmonics nearest it loud.** All the harmonics are still there. **Harmonics near a formant are tall, and harmonics far from any formant are short.** The outline of the harmonic heights is the **envelope**, and it peaks at each formant.
sub: During a schwa, harmonics near 500 Hz are loud, and the farther a harmonic is from 500, the weaker it is. Between two formants the harmonics get weaker, and near the next formant they get stronger again.
The harmonics stay the same from vowel to vowel, and only their heights change. So the **envelope** is what makes each vowel sound different.
Changing the vowel moves the formants while F0 stays the same. Changing F0 changes the spacing of the harmonics while the tract shape stays about the same.
blocks.end: So **pitch and vowel are separate**, because the source sets the harmonics and the filter sets the envelope.

blocks.main: **The formants of the filter depend on where the constriction is, and typical values show each vowel's pattern.** **Schwa** has F1 near 500 Hz and F2 near 1500 Hz.
sub: **/u/** has F1 near 300, F2 near 1000 and F3 near 2000 Hz, so all of its formants are lower.
**/i/** has F1 near 300 and F2 near 2200 Hz, so its first two formants are very far apart.
**/a/** has F1 and F2 both near 800 to 900 Hz, so its first two formants are very close together.
blocks.end: So the vowel shape is the filter, and it chooses which of the harmonics from the vocal folds come through loudly.

blocks.main: **Formants can only be seen through the harmonics, so a high F0 makes the formants hard to see.** The formants form a smooth envelope, and the harmonics are samples taken from it. Suppose the harmonics are every **100 Hz** and the formants are at **300 and 2100 Hz**. Many harmonics then sit under each formant peak, so the formants are easy to see.
sub: With harmonics every **250 Hz**, fewer harmonics land on each formant peak. A formant can fall **between two harmonics**, so it becomes very hard to tell the harmonics from the formants.
With very light, tight vocal folds, a formant at 500 Hz may have **no harmonic near it** to make loud. So the formant can be missed or unclear.
A higher F0 means fewer samples, so the spectrogram stops looking like clean formant bands.
The formants are the same in every case, but a high voice gives the listener only a few harmonics to hear them through.
blocks.end: So the lower F0 is, the more harmonics the formants can shape, and the easier the spectrum is to read.

blocks.main: **Very high voices leave so few harmonics near the formants that their vowels are hard to identify.** The vocal tract still has its formants, but there are not enough harmonics near them to show the envelope.
sub: A **toddler's** harmonics can be at 400, 800 and 1200 Hz. A **small child** of two or three has an F0 near 500 Hz. So only a caretaker who is used to the child understands the speech easily.
A **soprano's** harmonics can start at 800 Hz and continue at 1600 and 2400 Hz. So the words of an opera singer are often very hard to follow.
In opera singing the formants may not line up with any harmonic. Singers are even trained to shape the mouth so the formants line up with the harmonics.
blocks.end: That is why a toddler's or a soprano's vowels are hard to identify.

blocks.main: **A spectrum shows a sound at one instant, and a spectrogram lines up many spectra over time.** Speech is **time-varying**, because the tongue and lips keep moving and constrictions are made and released. Each moment of a spectrogram is one spectrum turned on its side.
sub: **Time** runs along the horizontal axis.
**Frequency** runs up the vertical axis, although it was on the horizontal axis of a single spectrum.
**Amplitude**, which was the height of each spike, becomes **darkness**, so the louder a frequency is, the darker it looks.
blocks.end: So the dark bands are the formants, because the harmonics near each formant are the loudest.

blocks.main: **Formants appear as dark bands that move as the speaker moves.** In **/ia/**, the two lowest bands start **far apart** during /i/. As the speaker moves into /a/, **F1 rises and F2 falls**, so the bands **come close together**.
sub: F1 is the lowest dark band, and F2 is the next one up.
blocks.end: So reading a spectrogram means following the dark bands as the formants change over time.

blocks.main: **In connected speech the formants never stay still, because every new sound moves the constriction.** In "Where were you a year ago?", the vocal folds supply harmonics the whole time. The tongue and lips keep changing where the constriction is, so the formants move from moment to moment.
sub: Where the vowel sounds like **/i/**, **F2 rises high and F1 stays low**. That is because the constriction sits where Mode 1 is moving and Mode 2 is springy.
During **you**, the formants **drop**, because rounding the lips adds mass right where the air moves the most.
Through **a year ago**, F2 goes up and then down again as the tongue moves from one vowel to the next.
Every rise and fall can be predicted with the same mass-spring reasoning. Find the constriction, then check whether the air there is moving or compressing in each mode.
blocks.end: So speech is not a string of steady vowels, and a spectrogram of a sentence is a moving record of the tongue and lips.

blocks.main: **Listeners identify a consonant partly from the vowel that comes after it.** A speaker said **ma** and **na**. The **m** part of ma was cut out and joined to the **a** part of na. The consonant came from ma, but **listeners clearly heard na**.
sub: The vowel's formants differ depending on the consonant before it. After **m**, one formant of the vowel stays fairly **steady**. After **n**, that formant **drops sharply** at the start of the vowel.
So the vowel carries the information about the consonant, and listeners decide which consonant they heard **during the vowel**, after the consonant is over.
This was one of the first striking results in speech perception, published in the **1950s** by the linguist **André Malécot**.
blocks.end: So listeners take in whole stretches of speech and use later sounds to decide about earlier ones.

blocks.main: **Speech recognition needs systems that take in whole stretches of sound over time.** The formants change constantly, so a network that sees two formants from one moment cannot understand real speech.
sub: For about seventy years, speech recognition machines treated each slice of sound by itself, and they **failed** despite billions of dollars of effort.

A machine that understands speech has to use the sound that follows to decide about the sound that came before. That is why modern speech recognition uses large language models built from many neural networks.
